# Module `collections`

collections - collection module surface.

The built-in `Vec<T>` (constructed with the vybish `Vec()` / `Vec(n)` calls)
already ships `push`, `pop`, `len`, `get`, `get_vec`, `clear`, `is_empty`,
`contains`, `remove_at`, and the array conversion helpers. This module layers
the first real keyed/set collections on top of `Vec` and the canonical
`Hashable` / `Equatable` core aspects:

  - `HashMap<K, V>`: a keyed map. Keys and values live in parallel
    `keys` / `vals` vectors; a set of hash buckets (`head` + a per-key `next`
    chain) indexes the keys so a lookup only scans the single bucket the key
    hashes to instead of the whole map. Buckets start at 16 and double (with a
    full re-hash) once the load exceeds 2 keys per bucket, keeping average
    lookup O(1). Provides `put` (returns `Bool`: false only when a fixed map
    is at capacity and the key is new), `get` (returning the native `V?` optional,
    consumed with `m.get(k) else default`),
    `contains_key` and `size`. Build one with `HashMap<K, V>()` (empty),
    `HashMap<K, V>(cap)` (pre-sized, still auto-grows), or
    `HashMap<K, V>(cap, true)` (fixed at `cap` entries, no re-hash, bounded
    memory for embedded targets).

  - `HashSet<K>`: a set of distinct keys backed by a `values` vector plus the
    same auto-growing bucket/chain index. Provides `insert` (returns `Bool`),
    `contains` and `size`. Build one with `HashSet<K>()`, `HashSet<K>(cap)`,
    or the fixed `HashSet<K>(cap, true)`.

  - `BTreeMap<K, V>`: an ordered map keyed by `Comparable`. Keys live in a
    `keys` vector kept sorted ascending (with a parallel `vals` vector), so
    iteration walks entries in key order and `get` / `contains_key` binary
    search (O(log n)); `put` inserts at the sorted position (O(n) shift).
    Keyed methods (`put` / `get` / `contains_key` / `size` / `iter`) are bound
    as `BTreeMapOps`. Build one with `BTreeMap<K, V>()`.

  - `VecOps` (on the built-in `Vec<T>`): non-mutating view helpers written in
    Vyb over the Vec primitives — `first` / `last` (head/tail element),
    `reversed` (a fresh reversed copy) and `find` (first matching index, or
    `-1`), and the ordering helpers `sorted` (fresh ascending copy),
    `min` / `max`. Bound via `Comparable` (which refines `Equatable`).

  - `VecHigherOps` (also on the built-in `Vec<T>`): the higher-order
    combinators `map(f)` (element-wise transform to a fresh vector),
    `filter(f)` (keep only `true` results in a fresh vector) and
    `reduce(init, f)` (left fold). They take a *non-capturing* lambda
    (`fn`) argument and are bound without any `Comparable` / `Equatable`
    requirement, so they work on any element type. The in-place companions
    `map_in_place(f)`, `retain(f)` and `reverse_in_place()` rewrite / compact
    / reverse the receiver through a by-ref `their<Vec<T>>` borrow; VecOps
    also provides `sort_in_place()` (Comparable-gated).

  - `HashMap<K,V>()` / `HashSet<K>()` (and their `(cap)` / `(cap, true)`
    capacity forms) are declared struct constructors: they return a fully initialized
    (bucket-indexed) instance, keeping the `Vec()` / `Vec(n)` construction
    idiom consistent across the standard library.

Import the whole module with `import collections` (the carried generic bind
methods reference the shared `samekey` / `hashkey` probes and `bucket_for`, so
a narrow named import of just `HashMap`/`MapOps` would drop those dependencies
and the binds would not resolve). `get` returns the native `V?` optional:
`m.get(key) else default` yields the payload when the key is present, or the
`default` when it is absent (no `Option`/`Some`/`None` ceremony).

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Higher-order `Vec<T>` combinators (non-capturing lambdas):

- `map(f)` applies `f` to every element and returns a fresh transformed vector.
- `filter(f)` keeps only the elements for which `f` is `true`, in a fresh vector.
- `reduce(init, f)` folds the vector left-to-right: the accumulator starts at
  `init` and `f` is applied as `acc = f(acc, elem)` for each element in order.
- `map_in_place(f)` rewrites each element in place.
- `retain(f)` keeps only the elements for which `f` is `true`, compacting in
  place and returning the surviving count.
- `reverse_in_place()` flips the order in place.

All are bound without a `Comparable` / `Equatable` bound on `T`, so they are
available on any element type. The `fn` arguments must be non-capturing (bare
function pointers); closures with an environment are a future extension. The
non-mutating trio never modify the receiver; the `_in_place` forms mutate the
receiver's own backing store by-ref.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    sort_in_place(self<their<Vec<T>>>)<Void>

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pure-Vyb `Vec<T>` extension operations.

The built-in `Vec<T>` already ships the mutation/access primitives (`push`,
`pop`, `get`, `set`, `len`, `clear`, `is_empty`, `contains`, `remove_at`).
These binds layer analysis/view operations on top, written in Vyb over those
primitives. All are *non-mutating*:

- `reversed` returns a fresh reversed vector.
- `sorted` returns a fresh ascending copy.
- `first` / `last` return the head / tail element.
- `find` returns the index of the first `==` match, or `-1`.
- `min` / `max` read the least / greatest element.

On an empty vector `reversed` is a no-op, while `first` / `last` (which read
via `Vec::get`) inherit `get`'s current out-of-range behavior (a known
compiler gap: the returned value is not a clean default). Comparison order is
dispatched through the `Comparable`-bounded `cmp_lt` helper (mirroring the
`equals`-based `samekey`), because a direct `compare` call does not resolve on
a generic element. The higher-order combinators live in a separate
unconstrained `VecHigherOps` aspect so they work on any element type (see
below).

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

### `BTreeMap<K, V>` · struct

```
struct BTreeMap<K, V> {
```

Fields:

- `keys<Vec<K>>`
- `vals<Vec<V>>`

BTreeMap<K, V> - an ordered map keyed by `Comparable`, bound to `BTreeMapOps`.
Keys are held in a `keys` vector that is kept sorted ascending (with a
parallel `vals` vector of the same indices), so `iter()` walks the entries in
ascending key order and `get` / `contains_key` binary search (O(log n));
`put` inserts at the sorted position (O(n) shift). Ordering goes through the
`Comparable`-bounded `cmp_lt` helper (mirroring `samekey` for equality), which
works for any keys that bind `Comparable` (Int, Float, Bool, String, ...).
Build one with `BTreeMap<K, V>()`. `MapEntry<K, V>` (reused from `HashMap`) is
the iterator item, so `for (kv in bt.iter())` reads `kv.key` / `kv.value`.

**Relationships**

- mentions [`BTreeMapOps`](#sym-btreemapops)

<a id="sym-veciter-t-"></a>
### `VecIter<T>` · struct

```
struct VecIter<T> {
```

Fields:

- `data<their<Vec<T>>>`
- `index<Int>`

VecIter<T> - a cursor-based iterator over a `Vec<T>`. Holds the Vec by
reference (a `their<Vec<T>>` view) and a next index, implementing `core::iter`:
`next(self)<Item?>` yields the native optional: present (a bare value) per
element and absent when done,
advancing the cursor in place through the by-ref receiver. Build one with
`v.iter()` (from `VecHigherOps`) or construct it directly. Consume with an
explicit `.next()` / `match` loop until the `for`-loop desugar ships.

**Relationships**

- mentions [`VecHigherOps`](#sym-vechigherops)
